rows.label: Value of a dollar given as cash, the benchmark behind "multiples of cash" (units of value per dollar)

source.title: GiveWell cost-effectiveness analyses, "Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly"
source.note: 0.00335 in 142 of GiveWell's sheets imported here (0.003355 in its November 2024 GiveDirectly analysis, 'previous estimate for cash'). A unit, not an estimate: the figure GiveWell's multiples of cash are stated against, so it has no range; GiveDirectly's own value (November 2024: 0.00872 in Kenya) is its model's result, not this unit.

rows.explainer:
What "1× cash" is worth. Evaluators state many results as multiples of cash transfers to GiveDirectly; the site turns every such multiple into units of value with this one figure, instead of each evaluator's own estimate of cash. It is GiveWell's long-standing benchmark, 0.00335 units of value per dollar (a doubled income for a year per $300), the figure GiveWell's multiples of cash are stated against.

GiveWell's November 2024 update of GiveDirectly's own analysis is 2.6 times higher (0.0087, Kenya). That is GiveDirectly's result, not the unit: the multiples evaluators published are stated against this figure, so it has no range.

rows.label: Cash spent locally: gains to non-recipients through local markets, as a share of the recipients' gain

source.title: GiveWell (November 2025), V2 GiveDirectly >6x BOTECs (the site's GiveWell GiveDirectly model, givedirectly-v2-6x-botecs-givewell)
source.note: Egger, Haushofer, Miguel, Niehaus & Walker (2022), General Equilibrium Effects of Cash Transfers: Experimental Evidence from Kenya, Econometrica 90(6): a local multiplier of 2.5. GiveWell's review of the study, after its double-counting, distributional, internal-validity (0.6) and external-validity (0.8) steps, puts the gains to non-recipients at 0.59-0.68 of the recipients' consumption gain.

rows.explainer: A side effect of cash, or of pay and inputs, spent in local shops and markets: traders' and producers' incomes rise, and where supplies are short, prices rise for other buyers. Reference class: the one large trial, Egger et al. (2022), lump sums to most poor households in western Kenyan villages, where GiveWell's review of the study puts the gains to non-recipients at 0.59-0.68 of the recipients' gain. The programmes that read this figure give smaller sums in thinner markets (remote forest villages, camps and crisis areas), where more of the spending buys goods brought in from outside and more of the rise is in prices rather than output: our judgment +10% (0 to +40%).
